summary: Describes how to carry IPv6 over IEEE 802.16 broadband wireless networks using the IPv6 convergence sublayer. It builds on the packet convergence sublayer for IP traffic. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: This explains how to send IPv6 messages over a fixed or mobile wireless broadband link called 802.16, a cousin of WiMAX.

subtitle: How IPv6 hosts talk over an 802.16 wireless broadband link, one point-to-point link per host.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.16 specifies the air interface, MAC and PHY, but not how IPv4 and IPv6 run over it, so IPv6 hosts and routers had no agreed way to use it.
tldr.mechanism: IPv6 packets are carried directly over the IP-specific part of the 802.16 Packet convergence sublayer. Each mobile station gets its own point-to-point link to an access router, with its own prefix, and some Neighbor Discovery timers are tuned for idle radios.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Proposed Standard. It has been updated by RFC 8064.

today: RFC 5121 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8064. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What the RFC Covers
sections.content:
IEEE 802.16 defines a wireless air interface, including the Medium Access Control (MAC) layer and several physical layers. It leaves out the details of how IPv4 and IPv6 operate over it. RFC 5121 fills that gap for IPv6.

IPv6 can travel over 802.16 in two ways: through the IP-specific part of the Packet convergence sublayer (IP CS), or through the 802.3 (Ethernet) specific part. This document covers the IP CS only. IPv6 over Ethernet and IPv4 over IP CS are left to other documents.

In the model used, the mobile station (MS), which is the IP host, reaches an access router (AR) through a base station (BS). The BS is a layer 2 entity that relays IPv6 packets over a point-to-point connection across the air.
sections.eli5: Radio links like 802.16 know how to move bits but not how IPv6 should use them. This RFC is the instruction sheet for the IPv6 part, using one of two possible doors into the radio.

sections.title: Convergence Sublayers and Negotiation
sections.content:
The 802.16 MAC has two service-specific convergence sublayers (CS): ATM and Packet. The Packet CS carries Ethernet and IP (both IPv4 and IPv6). A CS accepts packets from the upper layer, classifies them, delivers them to the right service flow and transport connection, and receives packets from its peer. Payload header suppression is optional.

Support is negotiated. After ranging and the SBC-REQ/RSP exchange, the MS and BS swap capabilities in REG-REQ and REG-RSP messages. IPv6 over the IP CS is supported only if the IPv6 bit is set in the parameter named "Classification/PHS options and SDU encapsulation support". The connection itself is set up with DSA-REQ and DSA-RSP, whose CS-Specification TLV says which CS the connection uses.

The 6-byte MAC header says nothing about the payload type, so the MAC picks a transport connection from classification rules. The IP classifiers look at the traffic class, the last next-header value, masked source and destination addresses, and port ranges.

The rules are firm. A host MUST be able to use IP CS when the MS and BS both indicate it. If both IP CS and Ethernet CS are indicated, IP CS MUST be used. The MS and BS MUST negotiate at most one convergence sublayer for IPv6 on a link. If they cannot agree on one, the transport connection fails and the host cannot send or receive IPv6.
sections.eli5: Before talking, the phone and the tower agree on which door to use. If both doors work, they must use the IP door. If they cannot agree, no IPv6 talking happens.

sections.title: Network Architecture and the IPv6 Link
sections.content:
The access router can be part of the BS, or a separate entity elsewhere in the access network, and one AR may serve several BSs. Between MS and BS, IPv6 packets ride a point-to-point transport connection identified by a Connection Identifier (CID). Several transport connections can exist between an MS and a BS.

When the AR and BS are colocated, the set of transport connections to an MS is one link. When they are separate, the RFC recommends a tunnel between the AR and BS at a granularity no coarser than per MS or per service flow. The tunnel plus the transport connections form a single point-to-point link.

Each link therefore holds only one MS and one AR, and each MS is on a different link. The RFC says this link is fully consistent with a standard IP link and fits the point-to-point link definition in RFC 4861. The point-to-point model SHOULD be used, and a unique IPv6 prefix or prefixes per link MUST be assigned.
sections.eli5: Every phone gets its own private road to the router. No two phones share a road, so each road gets its own street name, which is its prefix.

sections.title: Establishing the Link
sections.content:
The link is built as part of the normal 802.16 network entry. The MS first does initial ranging to become time aligned with the BS, exchanges basic capabilities with SBC-REQ/RSP, and authenticates using Privacy Key Management version 2 (PKMv2). It then registers, and capabilities are exchanged again; support for IPv6 over the IP CS is indicated by Bit #2 of the CS capability parameter.

If the MS and BS have confirmed support for IPv6 over IP CS, the MS MUST request a service flow for IPv6 packets. The network may also trigger the flow through pre-provisioning. Once the service flow exists, the AR and MS SHOULD send router advertisements and solicitations as specified in RFC 4861.
sections.eli5: The phone says hello to the tower, shows its ID, signs up, and asks for a private line for IPv6. Once the line is open, the router and phone start chatting.

sections.title: Prefixes and Host Addressing
sections.content:
Because each MS is on its own point-to-point link, each is effectively on its own subnet. One or more /64 prefixes SHOULD be assigned to a link and advertised with the on-link (L) flag set. A customer premise device serving several hosts may be the end of the connection. Prefix size and number are a configuration matter, and DHCP or AAA-based prefix delegation MAY be used.

The MS has a 48-bit globally unique MAC address, which MUST be used to build the modified EUI-64 interface identifier described in RFC 4291. Random identifiers such as those from RFC 4941 MAY also be used.

Duplicate Address Detection SHOULD be performed, but the RFC notes it may be redundant on this point-to-point link when two conditions hold: the prefixes the AR advertises are unique to that link, and the AR does not autoconfigure global unicast addresses from its own advertised prefix. Stateless autoconfiguration follows RFC 4861 and RFC 4862; stateful follows RFC 4861 and RFC 3315.
sections.eli5: Each phone gets its own street name from the router and picks a house number from its own hardware ID or a random one. Since nobody else lives on that street, double checking for twins is often not needed.

sections.title: MTU and Router Advertisement Settings
sections.content:
The IPv6 MTU on an 802.16 link is configurable, and the default SHOULD be 1500 octets. The MAC PDU length field is 11 bits, giving a total MAC PDU size of 2048 bytes. If the AR uses an MTU other than 1500, it MUST advertise it with the Neighbor Discovery MTU option.

802.16 hosts can go idle, tearing down the radio link, and the network must then page them. To avoid waking idle mobiles, the RFC overrides Neighbor Discovery defaults. The router lifetime SHOULD be large, preferably in hours: AdvDefaultLifetime MUST be zero or between MaxRtrAdvInterval and 43200 seconds, with a default of 2 times MaxRtrAdvInterval. MaxRtrAdvInterval MUST be at least 4 and at most 21600 seconds, default 10800.

The MS may send router solicitations at any time to the all-routers multicast address, but using periodic advertisements for movement detection is not recommended. Multicast Listener Discovery version 2 (RFC 3810) SHOULD be supported, and the AR SHOULD NOT send periodic queries to a host in idle or dormant mode.
sections.eli5: Phones nap to save battery, so the router should not shout "anyone there?" too often or it wakes them. The RFC tells routers to speak up much less often than usual.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it introduces no new vulnerabilities to IPv6 operation. Security of the air interface belongs to 802.16, which can cipher traffic on transport connections using a traffic encryption key (TEK) generated by the MS and BS after successful authentication.

An MS may still use IPv6 security mechanisms on top of 802.16 security. Security issues of the network beyond the base stations are left to the documents defining those architectures, such as the WiMAX network architecture.
sections.eli5: The radio link can scramble messages so eavesdroppers cannot read them. This RFC adds no new weak spots, and the phone can add its own locks too.
